sections.overview: The golden jackal is a medium-sized Eurasian canid: a flexible hunter and scavenger that also eats plant matter.
sections.identification: Adults stand about 44–50 cm at the shoulder, with a head-and-body length of 80–105 cm and a 20–30 cm tail. In Europe, males weigh about 11–16 kg and females about 8–13 kg. The coat ranges from cream-gold to tawny, with dark, mixed hairs along the back, pale throat and underside, and a bushy tail often dark at its tip. Long legs, a pointed muzzle and rounded ears help distinguish it from a fox. A small Gujarat, India sample averaged 8.8 kg for adult males (n=6) and 7.3 kg for females (n=4), illustrating population-specific sex differences.
sections.habitat: Across Eurasia the species occupies scrub, grassland, woodland, wetlands, farmland and rural edges. In south-eastern Europe, it often uses lowland marshes or mosaics of small fields and dense scrub: open ground offers food, while thickets provide daytime cover and breeding sites.
sections.diet: The jackal searches for food alone or with its family, seizing small mammals—especially rodents—as well as hares, birds, reptiles, amphibians and invertebrates. It also eats fallen fruit and other plant matter, and readily scavenges carcasses, discarded livestock remains and refuse where these are accessible. A review of European studies found that the balance changes with place and season: fruit is more common in summer and autumn, while ungulate remains and domestic-animal foods increase in winter. It combines active hunting of small prey with scavenging, often shifting toward the most accessible local food rather than relying on one prey type.
sections.behavior: The usual social unit is a breeding pair with the current litter; one or more older offspring may remain on the territory and help. A camera study of one Greek island family documented a stable adult pair and two yearlings that helped care for six pups, illustrating cooperation without making every group identical. Jackals mark and defend territories, and their complex howls carry between groups; in eastern Bulgaria, responses to broadcast calls peaked in summer, when groups answered together. Activity is chiefly nocturnal or crepuscular, although local disturbance and cover affect when animals emerge. Dispersing young can travel hundreds of kilometres to find a territory and mate.
sections.reproduction: In Europe, mating generally takes place in winter and births follow about 60–63 days later, usually in spring; timing shifts with latitude and local conditions. Litters commonly contain four or five pups, although larger litters have been recorded. European field accounts estimate that pups remain in a den, often an old fox or badger burrow, for about seven weeks. They then follow adults to forage and may return to the den until around fourteen weeks old. Females may mature at 10–11 months, but young adults can delay breeding and help raise a later litter. Both parents provision offspring, and older helpers may assist.
sections.ecology: As a mid-sized predator, the jackal takes many rodents and other small prey, while its scavenging removes carcasses and animal waste from some landscapes. The European diet review describes it as a potential consumer of crop pests, especially where rodents are abundant, although the size of this service depends on local food webs and waste practices. A north-eastern Italian study found dietary overlap with red foxes and partial partitioning of prey and habitat: competition is possible, but overlap alone does not establish food limitation. A recent continental model based on European playback surveys identified wolf presence as the strongest predictor limiting jackal occurrence; human presence weakened the modeled relationship, so this association does not by itself demonstrate aggression at encounters.
sections.conservation: The IUCN global assessment, published in 2018 and last assessed on 10 January 2018, classifies the golden jackal as Least Concern and records an increasing trend. In Europe, persecution and habitat change contributed to a marked contraction during the first half of the twentieth century. Legal protection in Balkan strongholds helped recovery from the 1950s, followed by natural expansion north and west. A 2023 European monitoring synthesis estimated presence across about 765,000 km² and reported expansion in 21 countries, while warning that reliable population totals are unavailable. France’s first confirmed record was in Haute-Savoie in 2017. The OFB’s March 2026 map documents scattered detections through 2025, with no confirmed reproduction in the country. Across Eurasia, local declines remain associated with habitat conversion, persecution or hunting, while the IUCN notes sparse data in parts of Asia.
